composition: Ferrite-based duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steel. The alloy class is defined by Al ~3–7 wt%, Mn ~2–12 wt% and C ~0.05–0.5 wt%, i.e. low C (0.1–0.4%), medium Mn (3–9%) and medium Al (3–6%), balance Fe. The specific alloy reported for this cold-rolled + intercritical-annealed + austempered route is Fe-3.5Mn-5.8Al-0.35C. Al is added to lower density (≈1.3% density reduction per 1 wt% Al) and stabilises ferrite, while Mn and C act as austenite formers/stabilisers; the moderate Mn and Al levels are what give the bimodal ferrite-plus-austenite structure with a relatively low austenite stability.
conclusions: Ferrite-based duplex low-density Fe-Mn-Al-C steels are a promising alternative among lightweight steels: a bimodal structure of clustered austenite particles in a coarse-grained δ-ferrite matrix can be obtained by process control at relatively low alloying contents, and the plastic deformation of the ferrite together with the TRIP and/or TWIP effects of the retained austenite can be profitably combined. This class exhibits an improved combination of strength and ductility compared with the first-generation advanced high strength steels and plots at the upper bound of the 1G-AHSS in the strength-elongation (banana) diagram. Because the hot-rolled microstructure (partially recrystallised, elongated δ-ferrite) gives high anisotropy, ferrite-based duplex steels are practical only as cold-rolled products, where cold rolling plus intercritical annealing (and austempering) is needed to control the final microstructure. The microstructural constituents of duplex steels are more diverse and their evolution more complicated than in ferritic or austenitic low-density steels: the coexistence of δ and γ, the different recrystallisation behaviour of the two phases, the partial reverse transformation of γ to α, and element partitioning during intercritical annealing allow many microstructural variants, and the final structure may comprise a combination of δ, γ, α, κ, martensite and bainite. The phase constitution, size, volume fraction and distribution can be controlled by adjusting the annealing parameters together with the preceding cold rolling and the following austempering, the key aim being to control the mechanical stability of the austenite.

aliases: ferrite based duplex steel (cold rolled + intercritical annealed + austempered)

mechanisms: Cold rolling followed by intercritical annealing refines the grain size of both δ-ferrite and γ and is used to adjust the mechanical stability and morphology of the austenite, because the coarse, elongated hot-rolled δ-ferrite alone gives high mechanical anisotropy and is not directly usable.

During intercritical annealing the austenite partially reverse-transforms to α-ferrite and C, Mn and Al partition between austenite and ferrite, so the austenite becomes enriched in C and Mn and depleted in Al relative to the nominal composition, which raises austenite stability above what the bulk composition suggests.

Fast cooling at 15 °C/s to 400 °C suppresses the diffusional decomposition of austenite, keeping the austenite metastable so that it can be further treated rather than transforming to ferrite and carbides.

Austempering (isothermal bainitic treatment) at 400 °C enriches the austenite with C by suppressing carbide formation during the bainitic transformation, so that part of the austenite is retained at room temperature; this is the step that enables the retained-austenite (γR) constituent.

During the isothermal/austempering treatment the γ phase partially decomposes by a eutectoid reaction into α-ferrite plus needle-like κ-carbide and retained austenite (γ → κ + α + γR); because γR/κ interfaces are coherent (mismatch <3%) while α/κ interfaces are only semicoherent (6%), the κ-carbides in this ferrite-containing matrix are thicker and more rod-like than the nanoscale cuboidal κ-carbides in austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels.

The bimodal ferrite-based duplex structure deforms so that most strain is accommodated by the coarse δ-ferrite matrix while the refined, homogeneously distributed austenite particles undergo a deformation-induced martensitic transformation (TRIP) and/or deformation twinning (TWIP), the balance between the two depending on the austenite's mechanical stability, stacking fault energy, grain size and crystallographic orientation.

The overall strength-ductility balance of ferrite-based duplex steels arises from combining the plastic deformation of the δ-ferrite with the TRIP and/or TWIP contribution of the retained austenite, which requires the austenite stability to be optimised through composition and processing.

For low-Mn/low-C duplex compositions the austenite decomposition temperature is high, so coarse κ-carbides can form already at hot-working temperatures as a shell at the δ/γ interface around austenite; increasing Mn suppresses this coarse κ formation, which is why Mn content controls which transformation products appear in these steels.
microstructure: At hot-working temperature the alloy is a δ-ferrite (>50%, BCC) + γ (FCC) duplex, with clustered austenite particles (10–40%) in a coarse-grained δ-ferrite matrix giving a bimodal structure. Hot rolling produces elongated δ-ferrite stringers/bands parallel to the rolling direction and refined, banded γ grains; during hot working there is C, Mn and Al partitioning between δ and γ with some γ→α transformation, so α-ferrite can form along δ/γ boundaries or within γ grains along dislocations. After cold rolling + intercritical annealing + austempering the final microstructure may comprise a combination of δ, γ, α, κ, martensite (M) and bainite (B), or some of them, depending on composition and annealing parameters. Intercritical annealing partially reverse-transforms γ to α and partitions elements between austenite and ferrite. During austempering/isothermal treatment the γ phase partially decomposes by a eutectoid reaction into α-ferrite and needle-like κ-carbide (γ → κ + α + γR), leaving retained austenite (γR) at room temperature. κ-carbide has an ordered FCC E2₁ perovskite (L′1₂) structure; in the lamellar structure formed along prior γ grain boundaries it is needle-like and coherent with retained austenite. Interface character depends on matrix structure: γR/κ and γ/κ interfaces are coherent (lattice mismatch <3%; κ lattice parameter 0.383–0.386 nm), whereas α/κ interfaces are semicoherent (lattice mismatch 6%; κ lattice parameter 0.387–0.389 nm); because of this, in the ferritic/duplex case the precipitates are thicker and more elongated/rod-like than the nanoscale cuboidal κ in austenitic steels. Non-stoichiometric κ-carbide was also observed in the ferritic matrix after isothermal annealing at 500 °C. For low Mn/C compositions the austenite decomposition temperature is high, so coarse κ-carbides can form even at hot-working temperatures as a shell at the δ/γ interface around austenite; increasing Mn avoids these coarse κ-carbides. For duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C steels the ferrite can order to B2 or DO₃ at low temperature, and DO₃ (which causes embrittlement) should be avoided.
processing: Process family: the ferrite-based duplex composition is first hot rolled to a banded δ-ferrite + γ microstructure (elongated δ-ferrite stringers parallel to the rolling direction with refined, banded γ grains), then cold rolled. The cold-rolled Fe-3.5Mn-5.8Al-0.35C sheet is then intercritically annealed at 780–980 °C for 50 s (the general ferrite-based duplex practice uses 700–900 °C), which refines the δ-ferrite and γ grains and adjusts the stability and morphology of the austenite. After annealing it is fast cooled at 15 °C/s to 400 °C to avoid decomposition of the austenite, then given an austempering (isothermal bainitic) treatment at 400 °C for 180 s. The austempering enriches the austenite with C by suppressing carbide formation during the bainitic transformation so that austenite can be retained at room temperature. An alternative reported variant of the same steel uses fast cooling at 150 °C/s to 500–600 °C followed by isothermal annealing for 60 min, which gives a polygonal ferrite matrix (recrystallised from δ-ferrite) plus lamellae along the prior γ grain boundaries containing fine α-ferrite, κ-carbide and retained austenite. Ferrite-based duplex steels in general are practical only as cold-rolled products, since the hot-rolled δ-ferrite is coarse and elongated, so cold rolling plus annealing is required to control the final microstructure.
properties: Tensile properties (CR + intercritical annealing + austempering, with annealing parameters adjusted): UTS 600–950 MPa and total elongation 30–70%. General hot-rolled ferrite-based duplex class (Table 2): UTS ~400–900 MPa, TE ~10–40%. A specific austempered example, Fe-3.3Mn-6.6Al-0.2C (quenched to 400 °C and austempered 10 min), shows a UTS plateau of ~610 MPa with ~27% elongation, versus only ~15% for the same steel annealed at 800 °C/5 min and water quenched, i.e. austempering gives higher elongation. Mechanical and thermal stability of the austenite decreases as its size and volume fraction increase. In the ''banana'' strength-elongation map the ferrite-based duplex steels sit at the upper bound of the first-generation advanced high strength steels (1G-AHSS). Characterisation of the class draws on optical microscopy, SEM, TEM, X-ray diffraction and thermodynamic (FactSage/CALPHAD) calculations; no hardness, fatigue, toughness or corrosion data are resolved specifically for this annealed+austempered sample.
summary: A ferrite-based duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steel (canonical reported alloy Fe-3.5Mn-5.8Al-0.35C) that was cold rolled and then intercritically annealed at 780–980 °C for 50 s, fast cooled (15 °C/s) to 400 °C and austempered at 400 °C for 180 s. The study/review question is how this processing sequence refines the δ-ferrite and γ phases, adjusts the mechanical stability and morphology of the austenite, and through C enrichment of the austenite (γ → κ + α + γR) leaves metastable retained austenite able to contribute TRIP/TWIP plasticity inside a coarse-grained δ-ferrite matrix.
unmapped: In this Fe-3.5Mn-5.8Al-0.35C steel, the thermal and mechanical stability of the austenite was reported to decrease as the austenite size and volume fraction increase, and non-stoichiometric κ-carbide was observed to precipitate within the ferritic matrix after isothermal annealing at 500 °C.

An alternative processing variant applied to the same steel — fast cooling at 150 °C/s to 500–600 °C followed by isothermal annealing for 60 min — produced a polygonal ferrite matrix (recrystallised from δ-ferrite) plus lamellae along the prior γ grain boundaries consisting of fine α-ferrite, κ-carbide and retained austenite.

Although the paper is a broad review, the ferrite-based duplex annealed/austempered route is stated to require cold rolling and intercritical annealing because hot-rolled ferrite-based duplex sheet has coarse, elongated, partially recrystallised δ-ferrite that produces high mechanical anisotropy; the δ-ferrite stringers and any δ/γ interface incompatibility are also identified as crack-initiation sites in these steels.
